beats.narration_text: Bonjour. This is Liam, in for Sanjiv. A decision tree keeps asking questions that separate classes. But how does it score a question? Gini impurity and entropy both measure how mixed a node is. We will calculate them on the same examples, animate their curves, and find a case where they disagree about the best split.

Preview node scores, weighted splits and disagreement

Test a disagreement with real arithmetic

beats.narration_text: Gini and entropy are different measures of class mixing. Both reward cleaner groups. Neither guarantees a better tree on new data. The interesting difference is how they score the tradeoffs between candidate splits.

show.event: Replace identical with different in the overview
Hold the corrected claim

props.text:
Gini and entropy are identical measures.
Both reward cleaner groups.

beats.narration_text: Start with the labels, not the feature values. This node contains four examples of class A and one of class B. Those proportions are eighty percent and twenty percent. A pure node contains only one class. A balanced binary node contains equal shares. Both measures are zero at purity and largest at an even mix. They measure uncertainty about the label inside a node.

show.event: Reveal four A dots and one B dot
Transform into pure and balanced nodes

beats.narration_text: Gini has a useful probability interpretation. Draw two labels independently from this node, with replacement. What is the chance they disagree? The grid shows all twenty-five equally likely ordered pairs from our five records. Eight pairs disagree, so Gini is eight over twenty-five: zero point three two. The formula subtracts the probability of matching labels from one. This is not the error rate of a majority-vote prediction.

show.event: Build a five-by-five grid of ordered label pairs
Highlight the eight disagreements
Reveal structured formula and computed 0.32

beats.narration_text: Entropy asks about average surprise. A common label brings little surprise; a rare label brings more. With base-two logarithms, our eighty-percent label contributes about zero point three two bits of surprise when it appears. The twenty-percent label brings about two point three two bits. Weight those surprises by their probabilities and the average is about zero point seven two bits. A class with probability zero contributes zero by convention.

show.event: Reveal probability bars and surprisal values
Weight each surprise; reveal structured entropy formula
Show computed 0.722 bits

beats.narration_text: Now move the class balance. Both curves vanish at the pure ends and peak in the middle. But their scales differ. For two balanced classes, Gini is one half; base-two entropy is one bit. Here Gini is doubled only to compare the shapes. Entropy rises more sharply near a pure node. Similar shapes do not make the criteria interchangeable when children have different sizes and mixtures.

show.event: Trace entropy and doubled-Gini curves
Move a probability marker through pure, skewed and balanced states
Label normalization and maxima

beats.narration_text: A tree scores the whole split, not just its cleanest child. Take eight A labels and two B labels. Send four A labels left, leaving four A and two B on the right. The left child is pure; the right is still mixed. Weight each child by its share of the ten records. Weighted Gini is about zero point two six seven. Subtract that from the parent score to get the reduction.

show.event: Partition ten label dots into four and six
Reveal child weights and impurities
Combine into weighted score and parent reduction

beats.narration_text: Here the rankings actually flip. Both candidate questions split the same parent: ten A labels and ten B labels. Split A makes children with one A and seven B, then nine A and three B. Split B isolates five B labels, leaving ten A and five B. The computed weighted Gini favors A. Weighted entropy favors B. Within each criterion, lower is better. Comparing their raw numbers across criteria is meaningless.

show.event: Reveal both candidate partitions of the same parent
Compute the two weighted Gini scores and winner
Reveal entropy scores and the reversed winner

beats.narration_text: A cleaner training leaf is not a promise about tomorrow. Watch a pure training group receive new examples with different labels. Neither impurity formula protects you from overfitting, noise, or an unrepresentative sample. Compare criteria with the same validation plan and sensible limits on tree size. Judge the predictions on held-out data using a metric that fits your task. The split score is a training tool, not the final verdict.

show.event: Show a pure training leaf
Send mixed held-out labels into it
Reveal validation and tree-size controls

beats.narration_text: Keep the distinction clear. Gini is the probability that two independently drawn labels disagree. Entropy is average surprise in the class label. Both guide a tree toward purer children using a weighted score. Their rankings can differ, and their numeric scales differ too. Choose with validation, not with the assumption that a more elaborate formula must be better.

ENTROPY — average surprise in the class label.
SPLIT — compare child scores weighted by sample count.
VALIDATE — lower training impurity is not a test result.

beats.narration_text: Try this prompt. Construct two candidate splits of the same labeled dataset. Compute Gini and base-two entropy for every node, weight child scores by sample count, and compare the rankings. Then explain why the preferred training split does not guarantee better test performance. Look for the child counts, the weights, and the arithmetic. Ask for a reproducible example, then check that the comparison keeps the parent data fixed.
